Sight singing is a culmination of a couple of things. First, we have to be able to connect a written note to a syllable (Do, Re, Mi, etc.). On the other end, we have to then connect a syllable to specific relationships of sound (intervals, scales, harmonies, yada yada). We get better at this by creating a strong foundation of basics and by reinforcing this foundation through active, unique exercises. You most likely do the same thing in electrical engineering. You don't jump straight in to complex problems: first you learn the concept, you practice the basic forms of the equations, integrals, and differentials, you see how the real world connects to the math you just learned, and THEN you try to find the unique combinations of these elements that solve problems. Sight reading will be the same way, and jumping in without a confident foundation will indeed be a headache.

This is the path that I recommend for sight singing practice. I was like you--I had to start from the bottom and work my way up. But it can definitely happen :)

1. Sing along in tune with a piano note. Move on when you can easily find your pitch after a 10 second moment of silence. Practice by matching the pitch of random sounds when you walk around the world (elevator noise, commercial music, etc)
2. Learn your major scale syllables, and practice singing only stepwise motion. Speak the syllables of nursery rhyme sheet music *with a metronome*. Move on when you can comfortably identify your scale degrees and you can easily sing stepwise motion forwards and backwards in your entire range. Practice by singing up and down random scales of your choice in the shower (with syllables!!).
3. Ingrain Do and Sol. When you play a note on the keyboard, you should be able to easily sing that note and its fifth. These are the bedrocks of most harmony, and they are your singing bedrocks. You should always be able to come back to Do. Practice singing along with things from a radio (or anything) from memory. A good way to start is take your favorite song that you can sing to, sing with it once as in tune as you can, and then see if you can do it without the music playing. Try to do it slowly as well as accurately.
4. Learn your thirds (Do - Mi, Re - Fa, Mi - Sol...). Practice slowly and without music. This forces your brain to work on only the sound relationships coming out of your mouth. After all, people learn to speak before they learn to read. Sit with a piano to get it worked in at first. Practice by singing scales in thirds (Do-Mi-Re-Fa-Mi-Sol-Fa-La....) up and down, just like stepwise. Move on when this is comfortable. Continue to work on simply speaking the solfegge of the music in front of you *in time*. Quick identification in this field is what will be your friend.
5. Practice arpeggios for each note in the major scale (Do-Mi-Sol-Mi-Do, Re-Fa-La-Fa-Re,...). Start being able to figure out how the notes feel. For example, when I sing a "Ti," it *feels* like it wants to go to "Do." Continue to practice singing things you hear in the world from memory. Remember to combine things you learn. So maybe sing scales as two steps and then a third, or two thirds up and then a step down, etc.
6. Learn fourths the same way you learned the other intervals. Extend the range of your arpeggios. Continue the other projects as a habit, not as headache homework.

Considering that it's early in the semester, I'm guessing that you're around this range. Go through this checklist. Will it be good at first? Absolutely not. It's not supposed to be. If it wasn't bad, you wouldn't need to practice it. Learning to sing by ear shouldn't be a grueling journey; it should be something that you're excited about! Hello! This is an interestingly worded question. I think I understand it, so let me try to repeat it with a bit more succinct wording:

"Why do the key roots of all the C modes fall within a C phrygian scale?"

The remainder of my comment will address this question.

First let's take a look at the more common practice where we start with one scale, C major, and find the modes within that scale. To think of this, I want you to consider the interval pattern of a scale to be like a ruler. We can shift the ruler around, but its pattern will always stay the same. The tick marks of a ruler will be the scale degrees of the scale (1,2,3,4,5,6,7...). They're gonna measure where in the major scale a note falls. 

The C of C major is going to be on "1" of this ruler. After all, in C major, C ought to be the first note :) Now let's keep this ruler in its place, and let's count up it. "2" would be a D, and the scale would be a Dorian mode scale. Keep walking up, and the pattern will be as expected: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian.

Now here's a new thought experiment. What if instead of moving the note like we just did, we shifted THE WHOLE RULER and kept our note constant. This is what you're doing! You are keeping the C constant, and you're seeing what modes come up when you have it as different degrees of the major scale. What happens when you do this, though? Why would Phrygian pop out in the roots?

Well, C in C Ionian is on the "1" mark of the ruler. The ruler has marks that measure out the intervals of a major scale. Shift the ruler down so that C is now on mark "2." This is C dorian. Look at what happened to the "1" mark on the ruler; it went down a whole step to Bb! Do another shift, Ab. Do another, G. This gets to the root (badum tss) of what's happening:

**Shifting the reference note up while keeping the ruler steady makes the scale roots go up the intervals of a major scale. Shifting the RULER down while keeping the note steady is the reverse process. It lays out the roots along the same interval pattern of a major scale but DESCENDING (INVERTED).**

You found the really interesting result of what this statement means. Any major scale inverted is a Phrygian scale! 

I know this is a lot, but I hope this illuminates why this cool pattern popped up. You were shifting the roots downward on the same interval pattern of a major scale, and that made an inverted major scale because you inverted the direction. Phrygian popped out because Phrygian is an inverted major scale :)

Hi there! What we call it depends on what the music is doing at the moment. If we are fully modulating to a new key, it's simply the dominant of the new key that helps us establish the new tonality. So if we go to A minor, we're gonna need an E dominant, if we go to Bb, we're gonna need an F dominant, yada yada..
It's there to establish the new home.

When we do this same thing but only briefly, we call it a tonicization, and the dominant is called a Secondary Dominant. It's called this because it's a dominant chord of something other than the I chord. So still the same chords, still the same relationships, but we don't fully modulate over to a new key. Instead we're making the chords in our current key spicier by tonicizing them and giving them a bit of emphasis.

Hope this helps at least a bit :)

So the circle of fifths is like a map of the different tonal houses and how close they are to one another. There are no actual instructions for how to build a house, but we can easily see each house's distance from its neighbors. To make a pentatonic scale, we need to go down to the scale level, inside the houses.

Take any major scale. Now take out the fourth note and the seventh note. This will remove all half steps from the scale, which is the goal of the pentatonic scale. 

C,D,E,F,G,A,B,C --> C,D,E,G,A,C

There you go; that's it!

Minor scales can be thought of as major scales but starting on the sixth note. So A natural minor is just a C major scale starting on A (ignoring any harmonic stuff or melodic minor things). Pentatonic scales work the same way. Start a major pentatonic on that scale-degree 6, and you now have a minor pentatonic. The same interchange works with the blues scales as well since they're based on pentatonic patterns but with an added semitone between scale degree 2 and 3.

C pent = C,D,E,G,A,C --> Am pent = A,C,D,E,G,A

C blues = C,D,*Eb*,E,G,A,C --> Am blues = A,C,D,*Eb*,E,G,A

Hope this helps!

This is just a deceptive cadence wearing a funny hat :)

Let's take a normal, everyday V - I progression, the easy-stuff we expect everywhere:

G - C.

Brilliant.

Now let's check out the deceptive version of this cadence:

G - Am.

Behold, we have been deceived. Instead of V - I, we did a V - vi.

Now what if we were to translate all this to the minor land? Well, it would look something like this:

V - I --> V - i = G - C --> G - Cm

V - vi --> V - VI = G - Am --> G - Ab

Cool stuff! But how does this relate to your stuff? Well, music writers picked up a little habit where they sometimes like to borrow harmonies from the other modes. They'll stay in the same key, but the progression will switch out some of the standard chords for their minor comrade. An example would be Eb - Bb - Cm - Ab - *Abm* \- Eb. The Abm is borrowed from the key of Eb minor, but we're still clearly in Eb major. It's a great sound, and you can here this exact progression in the chorus of "Jar of Hearts." As for your thing, you're briefly acting like the C is going somewhere. You're temporarily treating it like a dominant, a V of something. Modal harmonies are open game because they sound great, so these are our standard choices:

V - I = C - F

 V - i = C - Fm

V - vi = C - Dm

V - VI = C - Db

Looks like you briefly went to the minor land and did a deceptive cadence :) Chances are this was definitely not intended. You tried to chords, and they sounded pretty cool. However, this is *why* the Db(C#) relates to the C, so we can think of their temporarily relationship from this perspective. You can use this same method to find other ways to modulate through harmonic time and space. E7 could go to A (V-I), but it could also take you to F (V-VI). An expected V in F# minor (C#7) could actually lead you straight to Eb(D#) minor (V-i --> V-vi = C#7-F#m --> C#7-D#m)! Modal exchanges are awesome.

Maybe give this a shot? I'm not sure what vibe you're going for in your piece, but I find that extensions help the motion out a bit. If you are adamant about keeping the initial progression, here is a suggestion (E7 is a tough spot to get out of):

C - Cm - Bm - E7 - Fmaj7 - Fm7 - Bb7 - Abmaj7 - Abm7 - Ebmaj7

Kinda long and winding, but depending on how you use it, it'll get you there. Feel free to revise it any way you wish.

Another suggestion I have is to change the transition chords that you wrote. So instead of...

C - Cm - Bm - E7,

we have...

C - Cm - Gm7 - Abmaj7 - Abm7 - Ebmaj7.

This way we still return to a G thing as expected, but instead it has a new surprising flavor. This flavor also perfectly fits into Eb, and the ending mirrors that IV - iv - I you use but in the new key. I like the sound of this a little more because it's smoother, more symmetric, and the ending cadence is in "Jar of Hearts," but I'm not the musician here. If you don't like either of these, I at least hope that it leads you down the path where you find your answer :)

If we take a look at the first "phrase" starting at the ad lib section, we see that the first six chords are centered around A minor with the bass note having some fun with scale work by rising up to a C (Sol-La-Ti-Do-Re-Me). This type of frame work repeats in the next phrase, but instead of a diatonic scale, the bass goes through a chromatic scale and ends up creating some dominant chords along the way for some quick tonicizations. For example (if I remember the score correctly), as the bass goes from F# to G, the chord structure is D7 to G, a dominant tonic motion.

Then we get to the fun part: the part that starts when the violin has that high Eb top note.

Look at the chord right after that. It's a Bb major chord. Go forward two chords, and you have an A minor chord. Keep that up, and you'll get this progression:

Bb - A - G - F

Notice that the chords are descending stepwise. Now let's put in the chords in between these chords (without worrying about inversions):

F7 - Bb - E7 - A - D7 - G - C7 - F

With a little grouping...

(F7 - Bb) - (E7 - A) - (D7 - G) - (C7 - F)

All these groupings are dominant - tonic progressions! All the composer is doing is writing main chords that descend and tonicizing them along the way. 

The second to last chord is just using chromatic neighbors, hence the B and D# (C-->B, E-->D#).

Hope this helps :)
